opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the specific tricks are less useful than people imagine. When you work on RL for coding agents day to day, you end up with a long list of small things: how you shape the reward, how you filter tasks, how you handle long-horizon rollouts, how you stop the model from gaming the test cases. Each one matters in its setting, but a lot of them are very contingent. They depend on your base model, your infrastructure, your data distribution, even the time period. A trick that gave a big boost six months ago might be irrelevant now because the base model got stronger, or because someone fixed a bug upstream.

So if I just listed tips, I worry people would copy them without the context and either get nothing or get misled. What I think transfers better is the way of thinking behind them.

The first thing is that the environment and the evaluation matter more than the algorithm. In coding especially, the reward signal looks clean because tests either pass or fail, but in practice that's where most of the pitfalls are. Models are very good at finding shortcuts. If your tests are weak, the model learns to satisfy weak tests. So a lot of the real work is making the task actually measure what you care about.

The second is to look at the data and the trajectories yourself. A lot of progress comes from just reading what the agent is doing, seeing where it gets stuck, where it's being lazy, where it's being too clever. Curves on a dashboard hide a lot.

The third is to think about what will still be true when the models get much better. Some techniques are patches for current weaknesses, and those have a short shelf life. Others, like building good tasks, good verification, and good feedback loops, keep compounding.

So my view is: sharing the principles and the failure modes is very valuable. Sharing the exact recipe is useful for a moment, but it goes stale fast.

r001.rationale: The response says specific technical tricks are less useful than people imagine, highly context-dependent, and quickly go stale; it describes sharing exact recipes as useful only briefly.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the technical tips are less useful than people expect, and I say that as someone who's spent a lot of time collecting them.

Here's the thing. When you do RL on coding agents, most of the hard-won lessons are very local. They depend on your environment, your reward design, your base model, your infrastructure. Something like "we found the model collapses if the context window gets truncated this particular way" or "this reward shaping trick helped with tool-call formatting" — those are real, but they often don't transfer. Six months later the base model is different and the trick is irrelevant, or even harmful.

What I think is actually worth sharing is one level up: how you think about the problem. For me, the biggest shift was realizing that the environment is the thing. In the ReAct and SWE-agent era, a lot of the work was in prompting and scaffolding. Now with RL, the scaffolding matters much less, and what matters is: what tasks are you training on, how are they verified, how diverse are they, how close are they to what people actually do. If I had to give one piece of advice, it would be to spend much more time on building good environments and good evaluation than on algorithm tweaks. The algorithm part is becoming more commoditized. The environment part is not.

The other thing I'd share is more about mindset. Coding agents are a case where you can observe your own failure modes very directly — you watch the trajectory, you see where the model got stuck, you see it loop. That observability is a gift. A lot of the "tips" people ask for are really just the outcome of someone staring at hundreds of trajectories. So the real tip is: stare at trajectories. Don't just look at the reward curve.

So, to answer your question directly: specific tricks, moderately useful, short shelf life. Ways of thinking about the problem, pretty useful. And honestly the most useful thing is probably just encouraging people that this is tractable and that you can get surprisingly far with a clean setup.

r001.rationale: The candidate says specific technical tricks are less useful than expected, often fail to transfer, and have a short shelf life, indicating limited practical value.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re useful, but often more useful as examples of how to think about a problem than as recipes to copy. With reinforcement learning for coding agents, a particular trick might help because of the model, the tasks, or the environment you’re using. Change one of those, and it might stop helping.

So when sharing a technical tip, I’d want to explain what failure we observed, why we thought the change would address it, and how we checked whether it worked. That context is usually more transferable than the tip itself. Otherwise, it’s easy for someone to spend a lot of time reproducing a detail that wasn’t actually important.

r001.rationale: The candidate says sharing the tips is useful, especially as examples of problem-solving and transferable context; it does not judge that sharing them has little practical value.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re useful to share, but it helps to distinguish a specific trick from the reasoning behind it. A trick might work for one model, one set of coding tasks, or one training setup, and then stop working when those conditions change. The more useful thing is to explain what problem you observed, why you tried that intervention, and how you checked whether it actually helped.

For coding agents trained with reinforcement learning, a lot of the difficulty is in the whole setup: what tasks you give the agent, what tools it can use, and how you determine whether it succeeded. So I’d be happy to share technical details, especially failures. I’d just be cautious about presenting them as a recipe that everyone should follow.

r001.rationale: The response says the tips are useful to share and emphasizes sharing technical details, which contradicts the criterion that they have little practical value.
